text:
Introducing Sherpa: the most advanced fiction writing AI

We accelerated from $250M in ARR to $500M because Sherpa helped increase content production by 1200% in 1 year

Sherpa was trained on 5.5B hours of playtime with minute by minute dynamic retention data.

550K+ creators have produced 2.6M hours of content annualised using it

Pocket FM is like Netflix for audio-only dramas, with our own pool of one-person studios.

10% of eligible writers on Pocket FM make >$200K
One blockbuster produced >$100M in revenue
3 writers have become millionaires in <2 yrs

We built Sherpa to enable anyone to make >$1M by writing world-class fiction stories:

1. The Idea: Drop a 1-2 sentence concept. Sherpa interrogates it like a veteran editor on tension, stakes, and psychology
2. World & Characters: It builds out the complete lore, tone, and character psychologies
3. Sub-Plot planning: Breaks the premise into arcs, arcs into episodes, and episodes into scenes
4. Scene-by-Scene Generation: Outlines and drafts entire episodes, with you able to steer, rewrite, or override anytime
5. Editorial Review: Stress-tests every draft for pacing, engagement drop-offs, prose, and coherence before it locks
6. One-Tap Production: Pick a voice, convert to audio drama, and publish directly to Pocket FM’s millions of listeners
7. Global Scale & Monetization: Revenue-share on performance, with automatic localization so you earn across international markets

Test Sherpa for free here: https://t.co/R39M5o0Miz
_____________________________________________

Generic LLMs fail at serialized fiction because they lack a long-horizon narrative reward function.

Sherpa solves this through three core technical leaps:

1. Narrative World Model (State Tracking & Retrieval): Context windows degrade over long runs. Sherpa constructs an evolving semantic knowledge graph tracking character states, secrets, and plot dependencies. High-speed retrieval surfaces exact context on demand, maintaining zero continuity decay across hundreds of episodes

2. Hierarchical Story Planner: When writing a 500-episode story like Naruto, you need to plan 100s of sub plots. Rather than generating linearly, Sherpa decomposes narrative across discrete levels: season -> arc -> sequence -> episode -> scene.

Rather than generating everything upfront, like a generic LLM, Sherpa uses progressive planning and dynamic replanning. As the story evolves, it identifies what changed, traces the downstream impact, and replans only the affected parts.

3. Prose Engine (Trained on series' retention data): LLMs write robotically, but serial fiction needs emotion, tension, pacing, and dialogue that sounds like real people.

Sherpa's Prose Engine was designed specifically for storytelling. It was built on 1B+ tokens of Pocket's own stories, trained by learning from what listeners engage with, where they drop off, and what keeps them hooked.

Feedback is taken from specialized evaluator models that measure every scene against a 40-item checklist. (Evaluator models were benchmarked against human reviewers and matched them 80–90% of the time.)
_______________________________________________

Owning distribution and creation puts us in a very unique spot.
More shows -> More data -> Sherpa becomes better -> more creator success -> more creators -> more shows

Pocket FM has already seen one $100M IP. I believe Sherpa will soon lead to dozens of single-person studios creating billion-dollar shows.

Most people are scared of AI but I think it'll unlock more human creativity, help creators earn more, and bring the next great IPs to life. This will create millions of jobs and new income streams.

text:
Take the Leap, @Anthropic 

There's been a lot of debate about whether now is the right moment for Anthropic to complete its IPO. Markets are jittery, the calendar is crowded, the valuation conversation is loud. And most importantly, there are valid, serious concerns about the safety of these technologies.  But I want to make the case for why going public will be a net good for society. Not as a bystander, but as someone who took a company through this exact door fifteen months ago, in a sector that was  contested.

When Circle listed on the NYSE, we were operating critical financial infrastructure in a space defined by technical complexity, fast-moving regulation, and deep public skepticism. A lot of people thought the smart move was to stay private, keep our heads down, and let the noise settle.

What we found was the reverse. Going public didn't expose us to scrutiny we couldn't handle. It gave us the highest-standard framework in the world for demonstrating that we deserved trust. Audited financials. Quarterly disclosure. Independent board governance. Sarbanes-Oxley controls. Real-time accountability to millions of shareholders and to regulators in every market we serve.

The result wasn't fragility. It was confidence. Banks, governments, and enterprise partners who had been cautious about stablecoins could finally look at us through a lens they already understood. 

Going public wasn't just good for us and our shareholders. 

Public-market discipline turned a novel technology into legible infrastructure. But public-market discipline is only half of that equation. The other half is clear rules of the road. Innovation at infrastructure scale needs both: companies willing to subject themselves to transparency and accountability, and policymakers willing to define durable standards for how that technology can operate. For stablecoins, the GENIUS Act helped provide that regulatory architecture - moving the conversation from whether the technology belonged inside the regulated financial system to the standards under which it could operate there.

That distinction matters for AI. An IPO cannot substitute for fit-for-purpose public policy, and regulation cannot substitute for the discipline of public markets. They are complements. One makes companies legible to investors and the public; the other establishes the obligations, protections, and boundaries that allow an emerging technology to earn durable institutional trust.

AI is at precisely that moment now, and the stakes are higher.

Frontier AI companies are becoming core infrastructure for the global economy. Their model capabilities, safety practices, compute commitments, revenue concentration, and governance structures are matters of genuine public interest. Right now, most of that lives inside private companies, visible to a handful of investors and whoever reads the leaks.

An IPO changes that. It brings a frontier lab into the most rigorous disclosure and governance regime humanity has built. It forces clarity about risks, dependencies, and how decisions get made. It gives the public, policymakers, and the market a durable way to hold the company accountable, not through episodic drama, but through the boring, relentless cadence of public reporting.

Anthropic has built its identity around safety and transparency. The public markets are the institutional embodiment of those values. Yes, the timing is never perfect. It wasn't for us either. But there's a window right now where the world is asking hard questions about who controls the most powerful technology of our era and how. The best answer isn't a press release. It's an S-1, a listed ticker, and the accountability that comes with them.

We should be encouraging these great companies to take the leap to public markets, to subject themselves to public scrutiny and accountability, and we as a society need to do our part to hold them to the highest standards.

text:
At Zyfai we built adapters for every DeFi protocol standard (4626/7540) to restrict the receiver of these contracts to msg.sender.

As a project, we always thought about building session keys that can't do anything affecting user funds even if they leak.

Adapters are one of the pieces enabling this.

I'm surprised, but among most of the biggest protocols (AAVE V3, Morpho V1/V2, Euler...) using these standards (4626 or their own pools), none of them include functions that credit msg.sender by default.

This basically means that if you have a session key constrained to the target and function selector only, it can still pass any params it wants.

All the protocols integrated by Zyfai go through this adapter to protect interactions end to end. You can find them on our open source session key registry page here: https://t.co/RRmwxDs1tc

Today, a lot of projects still use session keys where they only limit access to targets and function selectors.

Pushing security has always been a priority for us, and I still think this is the best tech to build automated finance.

author: bubbleboi
quoted_text:
I am turning MAX BULLISH right now. Just like a river boat gambler holding his last chips I’m looking at the landscape and thinking fuck man we are in the fast take off stage right now.

I want to put it all max levered long on the high beta names and walk off into the orange glow of the sun. My bullishness has absolutely nothing to do with the math problems that are being solved most of them don’t matter that much. 

But it’s more the realization that every AI lab just had. They all woke up and said wait a minute what are we doing selling $200 a month subscriptions to idiots who are making slop apps and nonsense substack articles when we can just subsidize a few super geniuses by giving them real compute to work on an important problem.

No one really cares about navier stokes besides some CFD simulation cycles. But what if we put these compute resources on real valuable problems? That opens up a whole new world. The bull case for AI has always been to me discovering new drugs or even verifying they work/don’t work reliably… I was thinking way way wayyyy too small. 

There are hundreds of problems in engineering that if you got the experts in the room with real compute and even if they made a marginal improvement it would be worth hundreds of billions to the economy. Imagine we can build a steep slope device at 0.3V that’s worth like several generations of lithography nodes, or we can design a sub 100 femtojoul/bit optical IO and cut datacenter power by 40%, or even something as simple as more energy efficient molecular separation to replace distillation which is like 15% of all industrial energy use. 

This is the real shit guys. The labs are realizing quickly this is the REAL frontier this is the final land grab. Open source can never compete here because they don’t have the capital and resources this plays right into the labs hands. They can’t give everyone a 10,000 agent swarm but they definitely can give it to Exxon mobile and charge them $50M dollars for it if it means they find more oil or Dow Chemical to create a new kind of super glue or to Moderna to computationally create different mRNA therapies… the list goes on and on. 

A big reason why I never cared much for AI is despite all the normies going googoo Gaga over it is that literally they don’t have any clue what to do with it. Like if you were mediocre before AI you are mediocre after it, nothing changed u just got more skills that you don’t know how to use and you have no imagination or intuition. It’s the same reason why education is a waste on the majority of the population because let’s be real most of you aren’t going to be deriving differential equations or using epistemological concepts on your day job. 

But you give this kinda compute and unfettered AI in the hands of people who are world class. They will cook. It’s the reason why Deepmind has a Nobel prize and no other lab does because deepmind actually hired or worked with the top biochemists and biophysicists to develop alphafold. 

AI alone isn’t going to discover anything. Don’t fool yourself and grow up already if you still think AI is going to just figure out large scale nuclear fusion on its own then you are simply lost in the sauce at this point and are beyond saving. The pragmatic answer has always been use the AI to automate the busy work and keep the human experts for the actually thoughtfulness and intuition. 

I think the AI labs will wake up now and realize selling coding tokens and image models to normies to make Disney characters isn’t the best business in the long run. Actually using the compute for real serious innovation is and it’s really easy to monetize this upfront. 

I expect AI labs to stop looking like API companies and start looking like real research labs now. Thank god.

That creator of the Universe made us to be creative and innovative! He made a universe so expansive that we may never reach the end of it. 

So, go grab a telescope — have the humility to look up and take a moment to be in awe. It’s going to be okay!

text:
On the $ZEC Dev Fund debate:

The Zcash community has decided its identity is “encrypted Bitcoin.” It has rejected adding more bells and whistles to the protocol. To become encrypted Bitcoin, Zcash must become a dependable store of value, and that means eventually ossifying.

But the protocol cannot ossify now. Tachyon and quantum-resistance will take work. AI cyber hardening eventually requires full formal verification. There’s a final version of Zcash that will be ready to ossify. But it’s hard to imagine that happening within the next year or two.

The Dev Fund has done a great job and was a necessary step to protect Zcash development at a time when there was no private funding for it. But there's a reason why the Dev Fund was not set to exist in perpetuity; under current rules it expires in 2028. But Zcash has run up so explosively, the size of that fund is an order of magnitude larger.

I'm sympathetic to @maxdesalle's argument that Zcash does not want to become like a government. The political economy of slush funds and “grantmaking” is genuinely corrupting. The sheer size of the Dev Fund, given how much Zcash has run up, has changed it. A few million dollars of funding can be thoughtfully allocated by a few individuals, but once you’re $100M+, you must become an institution. Zcash’s Dev Fund is now precisely in that no man’s land that it will not be able to avoid becoming politicized. I think you just have to accept that, and minimize it as best you can.

I believe the fund has to exist, at least for now. There's too much work left to do for a deeply technical project. But who governs that fund is a separate question.

I agree with @matthuang that pure tokenholder governance is too volatile for a store of value asset. American citizens don't get to vote on the Fed Funds rate at the ballot box, and Bitcoin holders don't vote on code changes. Predictability is a prerequisite for storing value. Institutions can be wasteful and distasteful, but they are predictable.

I’m of the opinion that this should be the final Dev Fund. It's large enough to fund the remaining work until Zcash is ready to ossify, and then wind down rather than search for other things to fund. If other work must be done afterward, it can be formed organically by holders and allies, just as it is for Bitcoin. I don’t think it should move toward pure tokenholder voting, though I’d be supportive of something partial. Councils suck, but they are often the best answer to a messy question.

(Normally I don’t weigh in on Zcash governance, but @zooko asked me to share my perspective. Take it with a grain of salt.)

Disclosure: Dragonfly holds $ZEC and I'm a personal investor in ZODL. ZODL does not benefit from the Dev Fund directly, but you should know where my incentives sit.

A few thoughts on ZCash (disclosure: Paradigm is an investor in ZEC and ZODL):

- All blockchain ecosystems struggle with long-term funding, especially of public goods, and an inflation-funded developer fund is an elegant mechanism to do so. How this fund is allocated is a fair debate, and we should strive to improve it. But, we believe the dev fund is important, particularly in this age of AI cyber capabilities, rate of quantum progress, etc.

- As ZCash grows in acceptance and adoption as a private complement to Bitcoin, we think pure coinvoting governance introduces unpredictability that could limit long-term trust as a monetary asset, and it is better for the project to combine coinvoting with other forms of governance.

text:
Most tech giants in the 2000s built their infrastructure and product as one entangled unit. Amazon had the foresight to separate out AWS as an API layer, of which Amazon retail was the first of many users. Today, AWS generates more profit than all of Amazon's other business lines combined.

Hyperliquid is built with the same philosophy. Housing all of finance requires thoughtfully designed, open financial primitives. Each primitive should obey the Unix principle of "Do one thing and do it well." Talented builders then have the foundation to chain these together to create magical applications.

HyperCore borrowing is an example to highlight this philosophy in action.

Most other platforms implement portfolio margin by marking an account's collateral to market value with an LTV haircut, creating borrowed assets without an explicit lender. This system is simpler to implement, but misses a golden opportunity for composability.

Hyperliquid instead begins with a borrow/lend protocol on HyperCore. Every borrowed asset is sourced from a supplier, so risk is isolated within the borrow/lend primitive instead of platform-wide. HyperCore's portfolio margin system is implemented as an orchestration layer that composes borrow/lend, with other primitives such as perps, spot, and outcome trading.

This decomposition has several nice corollaries:
1. Today's announcement of manual borrowing is not a new feature, but simply an extension of the underlying primitive. Borrowers on day one have access to 400M and growing of supplied liquidity.
2. Portfolio margin users earn interest on their idle stablecoin collateral. This is not a new feature, but a natural byproduct of composing trading with lending.
3. System safety is easier to reason about when perp and borrow/lend margining are independent.

In the same way that math theorems almost prove themselves when the right abstractions are defined, composable designs just feel right.

“In-Context Robot Learning with VLM Agents”

Most robots need lots of task-specific training before they can do something new. This paper shows you can instead just show a general VLM what to do and let it adapt directly from context.

GPT-Policy essentially turns robot learning into prompting. So they gave the frozen VLM an example of the task, even just a human video with no robot action labels, and it can translate what it sees into robot actions on the fly.

This brings few-shot learning into the physical world, where teaching a robot a new behavior could look more like showing it an example than retraining a policy.

text:
Okay, I’ve got a video coming out, but here are my early thoughts on Jev. 

The first thing to know is that it’s not a large language model. It doesn’t produce text, it outputs decisions.

The decision types are (roughly) choice, score, and yes/no. 

It is roughly at the intelligence level of Sol or Opus for making these decisions. 

The question is: why are people so excited about this? A couple of reasons: 

The most important one is that so much of what we actually do in AI is making these types of decisions. Especially for enterprise-type work and AI harness-type work where we have to do things like classification and labeling constantly. This is things like deciding if this particular email is spam or if this person with an account on your platform is about to cancel. 

Within your AI harness, it's things like deciding which model you should use for a particular task. In cybersecurity, there are millions of use cases for this, where we're trying to categorize types and classifications of different inputs and the chances of something being dangerous, etc. 

When you step back and look down at most AI work, there is just a massive amount thatreduces down to making these decisions at scale. 

And that's the second reason people are so excited. 

This system is almost instantaneous and almost free. They're charging $42 per billion input tokens, and they are not charging for output tokens at all. That means you can make thousands or tens of thousands of requests in a lot of cases, like processing entire databases of customer interactions or processing tens of thousands of emails or whatever, and you might get a bill for like $0.12. Or maybe far less. 

And the round-trip time for making requests is in the hundreds of milliseconds. With an early sweet spot of around 200 ms. 

And when you combine these two, it means this system, or a system like it, is likely to be a new cornerstone for all AI work being done anywhere. 

The first step is to zoom out and take a look at all the different work that you're doing in whatever domain or whatever application, etc. Decompose how much of that work actually consists of making thousands or millions of these types of judgments and classifications. 

This includes your hook system inside of an AI harness, where you can do things on user prompt submit, before and after tool use, model routing, as I mentioned earlier: the classification and labeling of all your session data to find things you might need to improve or fix, etc. 

And then the next step is to essentially retool all that work so that it is going through one or more of these decision phases before handing off to an LLM. And it doesn't have to be one or the other. I have some implementations that are LLM-first, passed off to Jev for decisions, and then maybe back to an LLM, and some are doing kind of vice versa. LLMs and this type of system work really well together for tons of use cases. 

One of the things I've already made massive progress on, and that has me most excited, is fully updating my eval system to include this as a layer. 

Evals have two branches, roughly:

1. Asserts that are deterministic and very fast

2. Judgment, which breaks down into rubrics and tournaments

Rubrics are essentially center mass for this Jev system. They are basically a set of options that AI chooses for you based on the context given and how smart the system is. Like picking how happy or upset a customer is on a five-level scale. 

And then there are tournaments which have the system pick between two options, given the context and the intelligence of the model. 

But until now, these types of operations have all been done with LLMs, which are very slow and very expensive. 

What I, and many others I'm sure, are building is a way to have multi-staged evals where a vast majority of the work can be done by this system, basically instantly and for free, while shoveling out to an LLM if it is specifically needed.

text:
Take the Leap, @Anthropic 

There's been a lot of debate about whether now is the right moment for Anthropic to complete its IPO. Markets are jittery, the calendar is crowded, the valuation conversation is loud. And most importantly, there are valid, serious concerns about the safety of these technologies.  But I want to make the case for why going public will be a net good for society. Not as a bystander, but as someone who took a company through this exact door fifteen months ago, in a sector that was  contested.

When Circle listed on the NYSE, we were operating critical financial infrastructure in a space defined by technical complexity, fast-moving regulation, and deep public skepticism. A lot of people thought the smart move was to stay private, keep our heads down, and let the noise settle.

What we found was the reverse. Going public didn't expose us to scrutiny we couldn't handle. It gave us the highest-standard framework in the world for demonstrating that we deserved trust. Audited financials. Quarterly disclosure. Independent board governance. Sarbanes-Oxley controls. Real-time accountability to millions of shareholders and to regulators in every market we serve.

The result wasn't fragility. It was confidence. Banks, governments, and enterprise partners who had been cautious about stablecoins could finally look at us through a lens they already understood. 

Going public wasn't just good for us and our shareholders. 

Public-market discipline turned a novel technology into legible infrastructure. But public-market discipline is only half of that equation. The other half is clear rules of the road. Innovation at infrastructure scale needs both: companies willing to subject themselves to transparency and accountability, and policymakers willing to define durable standards for how that technology can operate. For stablecoins, the GENIUS Act helped provide that regulatory architecture - moving the conversation from whether the technology belonged inside the regulated financial system to the standards under which it could operate there.

That distinction matters for AI. An IPO cannot substitute for fit-for-purpose public policy, and regulation cannot substitute for the discipline of public markets. They are complements. One makes companies legible to investors and the public; the other establishes the obligations, protections, and boundaries that allow an emerging technology to earn durable institutional trust.

AI is at precisely that moment now, and the stakes are higher.

Frontier AI companies are becoming core infrastructure for the global economy. Their model capabilities, safety practices, compute commitments, revenue concentration, and governance structures are matters of genuine public interest. Right now, most of that lives inside private companies, visible to a handful of investors and whoever reads the leaks.

An IPO changes that. It brings a frontier lab into the most rigorous disclosure and governance regime humanity has built. It forces clarity about risks, dependencies, and how decisions get made. It gives the public, policymakers, and the market a durable way to hold the company accountable, not through episodic drama, but through the boring, relentless cadence of public reporting.

Anthropic has built its identity around safety and transparency. The public markets are the institutional embodiment of those values. Yes, the timing is never perfect. It wasn't for us either. But there's a window right now where the world is asking hard questions about who controls the most powerful technology of our era and how. The best answer isn't a press release. It's an S-1, a listed ticker, and the accountability that comes with them.

We should be encouraging these great companies to take the leap to public markets, to subject themselves to public scrutiny and accountability, and we as a society need to do our part to hold them to the highest standards.

text:
At Zyfai we built adapters for every DeFi protocol standard (4626/7540) to restrict the receiver of these contracts to msg.sender.

As a project, we always thought about building session keys that can't do anything affecting user funds even if they leak.

Adapters are one of the pieces enabling this.

I'm surprised, but among most of the biggest protocols (AAVE V3, Morpho V1/V2, Euler...) using these standards (4626 or their own pools), none of them include functions that credit msg.sender by default.

This basically means that if you have a session key constrained to the target and function selector only, it can still pass any params it wants.

All the protocols integrated by Zyfai go through this adapter to protect interactions end to end. You can find them on our open source session key registry page here: https://t.co/RRmwxDs1tc

Today, a lot of projects still use session keys where they only limit access to targets and function selectors.

Pushing security has always been a priority for us, and I still think this is the best tech to build automated finance.

text:
the most effective thing any longtermist can do to guarantee intended future outcome is to be around for as long as is needed to secure the future.

thus, the original milestone for any longtermist is winning a race against two contenders: mortality and existential civilisational crisis. but which should be won first if both can't be won at the same time?

generational stewards and succession planning are redundancies that have become the rule.

at best, every generation should have a designated offspring that is specifically raised to become the everlasting longtermist for when the time comes. this requires that the institutions persist throughout the ages to honour and execute the tradition.

but then you run into the risk of centralising power and resources into the wrong offspring and thus require careful engineering of offsprings or focus on more redundancies to grow the candidate pool. all while maintaining alignment, coherence, and eliminating dissent within/among the institutions charged with this mission.

you see how the simplest path is just to win in your time and generation then hope for the best? but hope is a dangerous thing and as deceptive as arrogance.

here lies our dilemma, a tower of babel or a golden path?

text:
This is where the $HOOKR thesis starts getting ridiculous in scale.

The SEC just created a temporary framework specifically allowing certain tokenized U.S. stocks to trade through permissioned AMM liquidity pools on public blockchains. That’s more specific than simply “RWA got the green light,” but the direction is enormous. 

Now think several steps ahead.

If TradFi assets increasingly move onchain and AMMs become part of that infrastructure…

Who builds and manages the logic around all those pools?

Compliance rules.
Dynamic liquidity.
Trading restrictions.
Oracle logic.
Arbitrage recapture.
Lending.
Collateral.
Automated rebalancing.
Crosschain liquidity.
Agent execution.

You could build every mechanism independently for every asset, protocol and chain.

Or you build a modular programmable-market layer where developers create financial logic once, projects plug it in, and builders earn when their infrastructure gets used.

That’s why $HOOKR gets so interesting to me.

Not “a launchpad with cool hooks.”

Potentially:

a multichain marketplace + infrastructure layer for programmable AMMs.

TradFi/RWAs bring the assets.
Uniswap v4 provides the programmable primitive.
Developers build the modules.
Hookr potentially becomes the distribution/composition layer.
OpenZaps/agents automate the capital flows.

And the SEC’s new framework explicitly requires things like auditable public smart contracts, permissioned participant access and trading stoppages alongside AMM liquidity, exactly the kind of complexity that makes modular market logic an interesting design direction. 

That’s the long-term bull thesis.

Not millions. Billions in potential infrastructure value if it actually captures meaningful adoption.

We’re talking about potentially helping program the markets that trillions of dollars of assets could eventually interact with.

$HOOKR to billions isn’t my thesis because “number go up.”

It’s my thesis because the addressable market may have just become orders of magnitude larger. 🪝

quoted_text:
WHAT IF robinhood:0x18e674231a58c239dc7daedcffe15ec3a24cff5c WAS KICKED OFF WITH UNISWAP ALL ALONG? 👀🦄

Okay. Full tinfoil hat mode.

What if robinhood:0x18e674231a58c239dc7daedcffe15ec3a24cff5c wasn't simply some random project that discovered Uniswap v4 hooks and decided to build around them?

What if the idea was kicked off together with people around Uniswap to solve v4's biggest challenge: adoption?

I have zero proof of this. Pure speculation.

But follow the breadcrumbs.

Uniswap launches v4.

Its superpower is hooks: developers can finally program custom behavior directly around liquidity pools.

Incredible primitive.

But primitives don't distribute themselves.

For hooks to truly explode, Uniswap needs developers actually building, discovering, auditing, composing and integrating them into real markets.

Essentially, v4 needs an application + distribution layer.

Now enter @NodarJ .

This isn't some random developer discovering DeFi yesterday.

His story goes back to DeFiZap in 2019: simplifying complicated DeFi actions into Zaps.

That eventually became part of Zapper.

Then years later he comes back with OpenZaps.

Same fundamental obsession, but upgraded for the next era:

programmable, bounded automation for onchain capital.

And THEN robinhood:0x18e674231a58c239dc7daedcffe15ec3a24cff5c appears.

This is where my tinfoil hat starts glowing.

What if OpenZaps was the underlying automation foundation…

…and Hookr was the vehicle designed to bring that technology directly into Uniswap v4 markets?

Suddenly you have:

UNISWAP v4
↓
programmable liquidity primitive
↓
OPENZAPS
↓
programmable execution / automation
↓
robinhood:0x18e674231a58c239dc7daedcffe15ec3a24cff5c
↓
distribution + modular hooks + Analyzer + marketplace + integrations
↓
PROGRAMMABLE MARKETS AT SCALE

And now Hookr isn't staying a launchpad.

It's pushing into existing assets, RWAs, other launchers, external builders and multichain markets.

That is EXACTLY where this gets crazy.

Because Hookr could potentially become an enormous adoption engine for Uniswap v4 itself.

Every Hookr integration = another reason to use v4.

Every developer building a hook = more v4 functionality.

Every existing asset opening a programmable market = more v4 liquidity.

Every chain Hookr expands to = another distribution surface.

And OpenZaps potentially sits underneath the bigger automation story.

Hookr proves the PMF.

Then other apps plug in.

Then AI agents plug in.

Then you get cross-hook automation.

One market triggers actions in another market.

One Zap coordinates multiple protocols.

Eventually capital potentially moves across markets and chains according to predefined rules, increasingly executed by autonomous agents.

Now zoom ALL the way out:

Uniswap = settlement/liquidity primitive

robinhood:0x18e674231a58c239dc7daedcffe15ec3a24cff5c = programmable market + distribution layer

#0xZAPS = automation/execution layer

AI agents = autonomous users of the entire stack

That's not another launchpad.

That's a possible architecture for DeFi 2.0.

So...

Did @haydenzadams  call @NodarJ  and say:

"We built v4. Now help us make hooks actually take over DeFi."

😂 I have absolutely zero evidence that happened.

That's the conspiracy.

But here's what makes the thought experiment so interesting:

If Hookr succeeds, Uniswap gets the v4 adoption engine regardless of whether anyone secretly planned it.

And if OpenZaps becomes the automation layer connecting those programmable markets...

The end result could look surprisingly similar to the conspiracy anyway.

Maybe we're not watching robinhood:0x18e674231a58c239dc7daedcffe15ec3a24cff5c and #0xZAPS build on Uniswap v4.

Maybe we're watching the missing layers that could help Uniswap v4 become DeFi 2.0. 🦄🪝⚡

text:
Coming into this article I was begrudgingly leaning toward coinholder voting as the least worst governance model on the menu. I liked your line that panels and coinholders work much like two chambers of a legislature.

Pure democracy still worries me, and I think very few have proposed it. Popular takes from the coinholder empowering camp seem to lean toward a representative democracy of sorts where the panel would be elected by coinholders. So I suppose I’d like to ask some clarifying questions to understand the differences between that representative democracy and what we have right now.

You mention that coinholders and panels should share a rough consensus to apply a change. The example for ZSAs showed that they didn’t go through because of how unpopular they were with coinholders. I think it would be more shocking though if coinholders overwhelmingly wanted it but the panel didn’t. It’s tough for me to think of a scenario where a panel would need to take a position to block the will of the coinholders. Do you have any examples to highlight why this might be necessary?

The other question I have is: how is the panel chosen? Right now it seems like the panel is chosen from those already on the panel? Meaning everyone on the panel agrees to add a new zcash organization such as valar, at which point they become a part of the panel also? 

Finally, I think right now all coinholders would agree valar group was a great addition. A no-brainer if you will. In a way the panel has the mandate of the coinholders because they have done such a good job. When there is criticism though, what mechanism do you foresee is used by the coinholders to override the panel? In other words what are the checks in the panels power (if any)?

quoted_text:
Safety refusal reporting is now available in the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index

In our latest Coding Agent Index v1.5, we’ve introduced safety refusal reporting to help explain model behavior and score differences. A safety refusal occurs when a provider or model declines to start or continue a task on safety grounds.

An agent may fall back to another model to continue, or stop the attempt with a block.

Claude Fable 5.1 had the highest fallback rates in both Claude Code and Devin Fusion, with fallback attempts accounting for 8.8% and 7.1% of the Index's weight, respectively; these results therefore include the fallback models' performance.

Refusal variability, harness context buildup, effort settings, and retry strategies can all affect the observed rates.

text:
Grok Bot summary of SpaceX CFO Bret Johnsen’s new interview with Tony Kim at SpaceX Mission Control.

Bret’s path
- Came from semiconductors (Qualcomm, Broadcom; was CFO of MindSpeed)
- Barely knew SpaceX / Elon when a board member called
- Thought aerospace sounded “old and stodgy” vs 6-month chip cycles
- Visited the rocket factory, called his wife on the drive home: we’re moving back to LA
- Now sits in the same magical factory: Dragon in the rafters, ~700 launches run from Mission Control, ~40 buildings feeding the campus
- Full circle: semiconductors again via AI / chips

---

Taking on AI complexity (during the biggest IPO ever)
- SpaceX DNA: run toward “impossible” challenges (first booster recovery felt like a rock concert)
- xAI acquisition in January + X + Cursor + Colossus = complexity multi-X in ~1–2 years
- AI is now the biggest business at SpaceX
- Bought time-to-market into the biggest product cycle of their lifetime
- SpaceX leadership DNA applied to that team
- Already feel leading on infra cost and speed
- Products moving: Grok 4.6, 4.7 soon, Grok Bot viral, Cursor strong
- Every week matters; soon every day

---

AI business: the money picture
- ~$100B company ARR exiting this year (annualized on December) — AI is more than half / the majority
- A year ago AI revenue was ~zero
- Capacity: a bit over ~2 GW this year → guidance 5–10 GW by end of next year
- Becoming one of the biggest hyperscalers, fast

Why they move so fast (vertical integration)
- Engineer the data centers themselves
- Act as GC: buildings, power, cooling, networking (plus partners)
- Used to regulators from rockets + telecom
- Removes margin stacking
- Talent transfer: launch-site / pressurized systems people onto data centers — Elon compared it to Yankees vs little league

Hosting model / ROI
- Monetize compute while catching up on software
- Demand knocked: “what are you doing with all that Colossus compute?”
- Short contracts: ~3 months + 3-month out (flexibility for their own future training needs)
- Payback: dramatically less than one year on cutting-edge terrestrial compute
- Hosting customers include tier ones like Anthropic, Google, and others
- Same watts can later flip to their own software at higher $/watt — optionality

Frontier models
- Moving maybe faster than anyone on trajectory
- ~5 serious players; need to be at frontier for recursive improvement
- Coding solutions improving dramatically
- Consumer vs enterprise tools will stratify
- Grok Bot: growing faster than anything they’ve seen; “transformational” user feedback; enterprise coming; expects roll into Cursor

AI safety
- Follow Elon’s self-regulation / peer-review path (like other industries)
- Logical, collaborative, including outside the US
- Hopeful something lands quickly

TAM framing (IPO)
- ~$28T TAM quoted at IPO; AI was ~$25–26T of that (digital AI only)
- Physical AI not even in that number — Bret thinks physical AI eventually bigger than digital
- Launch / space TAM = hundreds of billions (almost rounding vs AI)
- Connectivity (mobile + broadband) ~$2T — still small vs AI
- Differentiation: infra + X content (~500–600M MAUs) + consumer + enterprise push (Cursor etc.)

What to watch: Starship + terrestrial compute
Bret’s prioritization cheat code:
1. Get Starship right
2. Get terrestrial compute right for the next ~2 years until orbital kicks in
→ Transformational financially

Starship status
- Catalyst for all three businesses: space, satellites, AI
- Holy grail: full reusability → another ~10x cheaper $/kg to orbit
- Opens moon boots / lunar base / bigger industry
- Flight 14 later this month: production V3 Starlink broadband satellites — real revenue payload
- One Starship V3 load ≈ ~20× what Falcon 9 flew for Starlink capability
- Each V3 satellite ~1 terabit; ~50–60 per flight = enormous bandwidth per launch
- A couple launches start filling V3 planes; first-half-next-year benefits
- Eventually Starlink as % of global internet traffic
- Connectivity demand from machines (robots, AVs, agents) will dwarf human brains
- Same Starship unlocks next-gen direct-to-cell / direct-to-device
- Same bus + more solar + radiator + compute chips = orbital compute constellation

Reusability timeline
- Flight 15 may attempt catch / bring back first + second stage
- First stage already recovered and reflown
- Flight 13 soft splash best yet; recovered ship like a whale, engineers studied heat shield
- Reliable stage recovery this year; meaningful reflight next year
- Once a few second stages reflight → orbital compute cost can match terrestrial
- Then orbital cost curve goes down (tech / Moore’s law / aircraft-like amortization) while terrestrial gets more expensive (power, labor, regulation, cooling)
- Clean free solar, no community impact
- Industry agrees space compute is the future — debate is timing; others say ~decade; SpaceX flies first ones next year; meaningful compute in ~2028

Scale ambition
- Both cost and speed matter; near-term availability/speed most important
- On track toward ~100 GW/year by end of decade (~20% of entire US grid each year)
- Elon talking terawatt-scale in the 2030s
- Hosting proves staying power + virtuous cycle for industry
- New NVIDIA platforms: just fly the next satellite generation — no whole new terrestrial campus cycle

TerraFab (chips / memory)
- Parallel to orbital ramp, not after
- Not replacing NVIDIA — love the partnership; will buy all they can
- Worry is deeper fab / memory supply chain
- Memory industry ~30%/yr growth vs SpaceX wanting triple-digit — won’t work
- Hard technical challenge; memory may be early focus
- Want volume benefit by late decade (demo next year with Tesla development line → something in ’28 → meaningful ’29+)

Viewer Q&A highlights

**First bottleneck in the AI chain?**
- Chip supply for next year
- Power for infra players (utilities used to ~1% growth; turbines / blades constrained)
- SpaceX standing up investment casting for turbine blades themselves
- Orbital is the big unlock; squeeze every terrestrial watt meanwhile

How to tell durable AI spend vs keep-up spend?
- Bret: durability of revenue; diversified monetization of the same compute; host now, software later at higher $/watt; guided next-year monetization range ~$30–50/watt
- Tony: stack layers have different costs, margins, contract duration; SpaceX spans many layers with <1-year payback on infra

How soon a data center in space?
- First orbital compute satellites end of next year
- Meaningful compute in 2028
- Better phrase: “racks in space,” not giant buildings
- Same V3-like bus + solar + radiator + compute chips
- Already flown ~11,000 sats; launch + inter-sat + ground links already solved
- ~full rack (~72 NVIDIA-class) concept per sat; ~5 MW compute per launch

Tony’s investor wrap
- Still early; trends accelerate into physical AI and beyond Earth
- Connectivity / tokens increasingly for machines, not just humans

---

Bottom line in one breath
SpaceX is using rocket DNA — vertical integration, crazy talent, short-cycle iteration — to become a top AI infra + software player now, while Starship unlocks Starlink V3, direct-to-cell, and orbital “racks in space.” Watch two things: terrestrial compute scale (toward $100B ARR and multi-GW) and Starship reusability. Everything else is downstream of those.

text:
So @nockchain is going to reuse AI inference that is already happening at scale, to secure their blockchain

Inference providers earn block rewards and Nockchain's security goes way up. Win/Win

On Bitcoin, the mining work secures the chain only

Nockchain replaces hashing with zero knowledge proofs. Consensus does not care what you computed, only that you produced a valid proof below the difficulty target

So the miner and the inference provider become the same entity!

Lets walk through an example

🕐 You run a GPU

🕑 A customer pays you to run their AI inference request

🕒 You serve them the answer, and in doing that you produce a ZK proof of the computation

🕓 That same proof is your lottery ticket against the block reward

🕕 If it lands below the target, you just secured a block while getting paid by the customer

🕖 One job, two payouts, and the network gets secured by real economic work instead of wasted hashing

Nockchain already made chain improvements recently with Phase 2 (2.5 minute blocks and a protocol fund) but this update moves taps them into a huge existing increase in security supply while hitting the privacy aspects well

@Delphi_Ventures are proud $NOCK holders and we really like @loganallc, @chiefgrug and the team. They have persevered through some big hurdles and delivered.

讲一个暴论：
Robinhood Chain 的出现真正有意思的点，并不在于多了一条能打的L2，而是它把一类非原生协议的天花板进一步抬高了。

Uniswap, Lighter, Arcus(dYdX 的新产品) 的成功离不开它们选择跟RH Chain 深度绑定，事实证明这样的深度绑定确实有效地提高了它们原有的天花板上限。@flock_io 也选择了同样的路径和打法。

Flock 原来的主战场在 @base, 细分赛道是DeAI 的隐私训练和AI 模型资产化。这次选择在RH Chain 上上线FOMO(Fair Open Model Offering) 核心功能，本质上是在换分发层。

即将AI Models 变成RH Chain 上可发行、交易、使用实现闭环的链上资产，Flock 抢占的是AI 模型资产的生态位。值得关注的是，Flock 已和UNDP 多米尼加共和国办事处签订MoU 协议，解决政府和公共服务这种对数据隐私安全和可信度要求很高的场景的实际问题。

它们的打法出奇的一致：不是多部署一个合约，而是把自己变成链上细分市场的默认层。

Uniswap 抢的是公共AMM 的生态位，Lighter 抢的是perp 的入口，Arcus 抢的是股票代币化的生态位。而Flock 抢的是AI model 资产化的生态位。

可以预见的是，Flock 之后，一定还会有更多的非原生协议选择深度绑定RH Chain。

而真正的Robinhood Summer，还远没有到来。
author: y_cryptoanalyst
quoted_text:
关于Robinhood Chain 的热度能否持续，X 上已经出现了明显的分歧。

我个人的观点非常明确：RH Chain 生态的叙事是继铭文叙事后的又一个长周期叙事，目前仍处在较早的发酵期。

Robinhood 的热点并非单点驱动，而是meme, NFT, 币股，defi 多点开花此起彼伏，总能够在热度稍降下来就迅速续上。

而这一切还是发生在强敌林立且极度内卷的公链大环境下，不乏Solana, Base, HyperEVM 这些强劲的对手。强资源驱动，可想而之RH Chain 背后有多强的资源。

那RH Chain 的底层技术是足够卓越吗？答案是否定的，它甚至不能称之为一条有技术创新的L2 链。从L2beat 的分级、从近期高昂的gas、从它们从不宣扬自己的技术就能看出来。

但就是这样一条毫无技术优势的L2 链，把向来自视甚高的Base 打得毫无还手之力，而且还是在Base 拿着一张发币预期的王牌的前提下。

这样的一条链你跟我说它只有1个多月的高光期？恕不敢苟同。

🧠 What’s Really Going On in Machine Learning? Some Minimal Models
Stephen Wolfram

📖 Get the book: https://t.co/WBjdLLGvaX

🤯 Why does machine learning work at all?

Neural networks power everything from image recognition to language models—but the deeper question of why these systems can learn remains surprisingly difficult to answer.

In What’s Really Going On in Machine Learning?, Stephen Wolfram strips machine learning down to minimal models built from simple rules and explores what happens when even these basic systems are allowed to learn.

🔬 Explore the ideas behind:
• Why simple systems can exhibit learning
• Minimal models of machine learning
• The role of computational complexity
• Sampling complexity & why learning works
• Neural networks and their surprising behavior
• Why some AI successes resist simple explanations
• The limits of our current understanding of AI
• Whether machine learning can ever have a single unifying theory

💡 The central insight:
Machine learning may be less about carefully engineered structures and more about the underlying complexity of computation itself.

Rather than offering another recipe for building AI, Wolfram takes a step back and asks a deeper question: what is really happening underneath the machinery of learning?

🎯 Perfect for:
AI researchers, ML practitioners, computer scientists, mathematicians, students, and curious readers interested in the foundations and limits of machine learning.

🚀 Go beneath the algorithms—and question what it actually means for a machine to learn.

text:
马斯克刚刚说美国GDP 明年开始两倍增速到约4%。

这句话其实比看起来更夸张，但先别理解错：他说的不是美国GDP明年翻倍，而是GDP增速从约2%提高到4%。

对美国这种体量的经济体来说，多出来的2个百分点，就是数千亿美元级别的额外经济产出。真正的赌注也不是“AI模型会不会更聪明”，而是AI能不能在一年内从科技公司扩散到代码、客服、金融、研发、制造，真正提高整个经济的人均产出。

而且4%明显高于目前主流预测——美联储最新对2027年的预测大约只有 2.4%。

如果马斯克是对的，AI就不再只是一个“科技股故事”，而是在开始改变美国经济本身。

但这里还有一个反直觉的问题：如果AI真的把GDP推到4%，美联储还需要降息吗？

author: ndrewpignanelli
quoted_text:
The cost of legal services is approaching $0. I've mostly seen two ways to monetize this theme: (1) selling tokens to law firms (@WeAreLegora & @harvey) who "resell those tokens" to their clients, and (2) providing legal services on your own to businesses or consumers at a much lower cost profile & taking on more clients. 

One thing I haven't yet seen is how to express this theme in other industries on the assumption that legal services are trending to $0. 

In a world where you have unlimited free lawyers, what are the opportunities to do things that you wouldn't otherwise be able to do? Some ideas: 

One idea is flavors of investing that are heavy on interfacing with legal/regulatory challenges i.e. public activism. On an adjacent note, buying B2B receivables and then using AI to collect. 

Interesting to think about the others. Especially with the advent of long running agents, opportunity set increases with ability to answer emails and engage with adversarial processes in a way that seemed harder before. Muse & Instinct feel like a first taste into what's possible.

author: ChainLinkGod
quoted_text:
The end-state for crypto tokens is protocol equity

A digital asset that serves as a claim on the future positive cash flows of a blockchain-based protocol

That’s it, this is how tokens accrue value, no ponzinomics or mental gymnastics required

1. Solve a real problem for a large addressable market

2. Monetize adoption as dominant market share is achieved

3. Accrue value to token via a dividend (staking reward) and/or a buy-back (token burn)

Not every protocol will succeed and become cash flow positive, but those that do, present the largest opportunity for token investors

This has largely not occurred to date due to the openly and aggressively hostile U.S. regulatory environment toward crypto

Projects that fly too close to the sun risk putting themselves in the direct cross-hairs of government agencies looking to make an example of an industry they (falsely) perceive as a threat

Hence, instead of protocol equity, we have “utility tokens” or “governance tokens” to mask what the ultimate end goal is

This is obviously unsustainable, hence the extreme volatility as people don’t know how to price these assets, while raw speculation keeps the market alive

Thankfully, we are starting to see a shift in attitude within the U.S., mainly from politicians who are taking note of who is writing the major checks this election cycle

Once the regulatory environment clears up, however long that may take, we can finally enter the next stage of crypto’s evolution:

I was going to write this one for subscribers, but I have to make this for everyone because so many people still don't see the vision

I still think robinhood:0xaa07a0e9209e16ac99708c3ec70159c6ef3128a3 is the most asymmetric project on Robinhood Chain. This is a net-new vertical, with all the right levers in a world where AI demand is accelerating.

Yes, inference marketplaces have been tried in crypto. But none have worked at scale. With CREDIT, akin to DIEM, you now have succeeded at tokenizing inference. And in doing so, you basically unlock credits for an increasingly agentic world. Agents need fuel they can buy and use without a human in the loop; This is the start of inference as an onchain commodity. 

This is obviously a pro-sumer application; but that's fine because the largest winners of AI inference are individuals and small teams, not enterprises. Enterprises are either A) developing in-house model harnesses for privacy purposes, or B) have infinite budget for AI

And people treat that like a bear case - I don't see a problem with being for consumers. The TAM for consumer inference is still huge - Menlo Ventures State of Consumer AI est. 1.7b - 1.8b use AI tools ; at $20/m that's 432b a year. Also, in their enterprise report, product-led growth drives 27% of AI spend, and shadow AI (employees paying on their own) pushes that closer to 40%. Cursor hit $200M in revenue before hiring a single enterprise sales rep. 

There is a clear latent demand for cheap inference amongst pro-sumers. The unlocks are clear - it can become the payment layer for AI agents; More users buying credits leads to more demand for CREDIT, which makes staking ORBIO more valuable, which raises the ORBIO price, which creates more trading fees, which funds more discounts, which brings in more users. As long as it keeps spinning, each part feeds the others.

It combines three hot themes: AI agents, tokenized real-world assets, and Robinhood Chain. The NVDA-linked fee route adds to that. In a strong market, a story this clean can attract a lot of capital, which itself funds the subsidy for longer.

And of course, above it all, the man pushing this himself - @0x_aster is a cracked dev who has shown his capabililties are far beyond the norm; Multiple updates within a week, clear direction - this is founder-market fit. 

In crypto, actions carry way more weight than words. And look at what he's shipped man... a working gateway, a live orderbook, and now tokenized inference. The man is A MACHINE. This is what AI x strong founders can do - go beyond 10x engineer to become a 10,000x engineer. HE'S CRACKED!

Founder-market fit matters more in this sector than most. A team that ships slowly gets left behind by the market itself. 

And for the bear takes:

Q: DIEM already does this, why do we need another one

- DIEM is precisely the success case. VVV is valued at 1B. ORBIO is valued at 15m. Also, VVV is going in the direction of private AI. ORBIO is going in the direction of serving the layer of inference for consumers across the world. CREDIT is $1 of usage you hold until you need it. Burst-heavy users (agents running a big job, devs shipping a feature) don't use the same amount every day. They need compute they can stockpile, buy at a discount, and spend in one go.

Lastly, markets rarely have one winner. Stablecoins didn't stop at USDT. Venice proved people will pay for tokenized inference. There is room for a second design.

Q: It's just an OpenRouter reseller. There's no moat.

Fair take. Yes, bits can be copied, there's no moat there. The moat is the market - liquidity begets liquidity in any marketplace. There's 20 different perp dexes. Who wins? The most liquid markets with the most volume traded on it. 

And obv there is no confirmed answer, but ultimately, that's what markets are - I'm betting on this

Q: "They could be shut down"

This is the most legitimate bear take, yes. Platform risk is real for any aggregator. But labs want volume, and resellers bring demand they wouldn't otherwise get. Venice has run Claude, GPT and Gemini through a token model at scale, which suggests it can work.

But on top of that, as the world moves towards open source, this becomes less and less of a risk ;

Anyways, send it

bonsai 2 27b just built this from one paragraph of prompt in one shot, all of it out of a 5.9gb file on an rtx 3060 12gb.

i did not expect frontend taste at this size. small models usually get the logic right and the layout wrong, this one got the layout right, and it thought for a long time to do it, 41k tokens over 46 minutes, the context ran out to 77k and it never lost the thread.

this is a ternary compression of qwen 3.8 27b, 26 tok/s fresh on a five year old gaming gpu, 13 tok/s at 77k deep, the whole 262k window resident. for what it is, on this card, this is insane, and i cannot wait to run it through real agentic coding on hermes agent, the tool loop, the builds that break and have to recover.

@PrismML keep going, this is the one that runs on the card people actually own.
author: PrismML
quoted_text:
bonsai 2 27b on an rtx 3060 12gb, the full receipt sheet. save this one, the 12gb row of the small gpu guide is built from it.

speed by depth, then what context costs, live server, thinking on, real sessions
> 7k deep: 24.4 tok/s
> 12k deep: 21.9 tok/s
> 35k deep: 17.8 tok/s
> 77k deep: 13.0 tok/s
> 64k window: 7.3gb resident
> 128k window: 8.8gb resident
> 192k window: 10.2gb resident
> 262k window: 11.7gb resident, 0.6gb to spare, the whole native window on a 12gb card
> every 64k of context costs 1.47gb, so 327k would not fit
> a 41,312 token build session from 35k to 77k of context averaged 15.0 tok/s across 46 minutes
> prefill 295 tok/s at 2k of context, 243 tok/s at 35k, first token in 0.6 seconds, fresh decode 26.1 tok/s
> the card pinned 149 of 150 w the entire time, 78c, fan at 80%, power bound, not heat bound
> 0.158 tok/s per watt at the fresh end

the setup
> model: ternary bonsai 2 27b, PTQ1_0, 1.75 bits per weight, 5.95gb on disk, base qwen 3.8 27b, apache 2.0
> runtime: prismml llama.cpp fork, prebuilt cuda 12.4 binary, no compile
> serve: full 262k native window resident, q4 kv cache, flash attention, one slot, 11.7 of 12gb in use

for anyone who followed bonsai 1 in july, that was the 3.9gb 1bit file at 42 tok/s on a 3060 ti, a faster card and a smaller file, so the same card comparison is not on the table yet, it comes with the 8gb test. 

what changed is the base, qwen 3.8 instead of 3.6, and the retention, 98.2% on their suite instead of 95%, and the whole 262k window fitting on 12gb.

Here’s how to check if your 𝕏 account is shadowbanned or has any visibility labels limiting the reach of your account or posts:

1) Open https://t.co/271Oc9GcSc
2) Click “Download”
3) Open the downloaded JSON file in any browser or text editor

How to read the report:

• period: The dates covered by the report
• generatedAt: When the report was created
• postCount: Number of posts analyzed during that period
• postLabels: Visibility labels applied to individual posts
• accountLabels: Visibility labels applied to your account
• totalPostLabels: Total post-level labels
• totalAccountLabels: Total account-level labels

An empty bracket [] means no labels are listed. If both totals show 0, no post or account visibility labels were recorded during that reporting period.

Note: If the link is not working for you, the feature is still rolling out to more eligible users. You can check again later.

𝕏 lets users inspect this information instead of leaving them guessing. This is real transparency.

quoted_text:
I was going to write this one for subscribers, but I have to make this for everyone because so many people still don't see the vision

I still think robinhood:0xaa07a0e9209e16ac99708c3ec70159c6ef3128a3 is the most asymmetric project on Robinhood Chain. This is a net-new vertical, with all the right levers in a world where AI demand is accelerating.

Yes, inference marketplaces have been tried in crypto. But none have worked at scale. With CREDIT, akin to DIEM, you now have succeeded at tokenizing inference. And in doing so, you basically unlock credits for an increasingly agentic world. Agents need fuel they can buy and use without a human in the loop; This is the start of inference as an onchain commodity. 

This is obviously a pro-sumer application; but that's fine because the largest winners of AI inference are individuals and small teams, not enterprises. Enterprises are either A) developing in-house model harnesses for privacy purposes, or B) have infinite budget for AI

And people treat that like a bear case - I don't see a problem with being for consumers. The TAM for consumer inference is still huge - Menlo Ventures State of Consumer AI est. 1.7b - 1.8b use AI tools ; at $20/m that's 432b a year. Also, in their enterprise report, product-led growth drives 27% of AI spend, and shadow AI (employees paying on their own) pushes that closer to 40%. Cursor hit $200M in revenue before hiring a single enterprise sales rep. 

There is a clear latent demand for cheap inference amongst pro-sumers. The unlocks are clear - it can become the payment layer for AI agents; More users buying credits leads to more demand for CREDIT, which makes staking ORBIO more valuable, which raises the ORBIO price, which creates more trading fees, which funds more discounts, which brings in more users. As long as it keeps spinning, each part feeds the others.

It combines three hot themes: AI agents, tokenized real-world assets, and Robinhood Chain. The NVDA-linked fee route adds to that. In a strong market, a story this clean can attract a lot of capital, which itself funds the subsidy for longer.

And of course, above it all, the man pushing this himself - @0x_aster is a cracked dev who has shown his capabililties are far beyond the norm; Multiple updates within a week, clear direction - this is founder-market fit. 

In crypto, actions carry way more weight than words. And look at what he's shipped man... a working gateway, a live orderbook, and now tokenized inference. The man is A MACHINE. This is what AI x strong founders can do - go beyond 10x engineer to become a 10,000x engineer. HE'S CRACKED!

Founder-market fit matters more in this sector than most. A team that ships slowly gets left behind by the market itself. 

And for the bear takes:

Q: DIEM already does this, why do we need another one

- DIEM is precisely the success case. VVV is valued at 1B. ORBIO is valued at 15m. Also, VVV is going in the direction of private AI. ORBIO is going in the direction of serving the layer of inference for consumers across the world. CREDIT is $1 of usage you hold until you need it. Burst-heavy users (agents running a big job, devs shipping a feature) don't use the same amount every day. They need compute they can stockpile, buy at a discount, and spend in one go.

Lastly, markets rarely have one winner. Stablecoins didn't stop at USDT. Venice proved people will pay for tokenized inference. There is room for a second design.

Q: It's just an OpenRouter reseller. There's no moat.

Fair take. Yes, bits can be copied, there's no moat there. The moat is the market - liquidity begets liquidity in any marketplace. There's 20 different perp dexes. Who wins? The most liquid markets with the most volume traded on it. 

And obv there is no confirmed answer, but ultimately, that's what markets are - I'm betting on this

Q: "They could be shut down"

This is the most legitimate bear take, yes. Platform risk is real for any aggregator. But labs want volume, and resellers bring demand they wouldn't otherwise get. Venice has run Claude, GPT and Gemini through a token model at scale, which suggests it can work.

But on top of that, as the world moves towards open source, this becomes less and less of a risk ;

Anyways, send it

text:
Something I wanted to clarify now that the manga is out:

Over the years, we’ve told Azuki stories in different formats. With the manga, we’ve found the format we want as the primary driver of the story. So what does that mean for things like the Shao 2.5D short? What’s “canon”?

The manga is a new endeavor for me, especially on the writing side, so I wanted to maintain as much creative flexibility as possible. There were a few things I knew we had to preserve: the characters, the setting, red beans and gates, and the spirit of the story between the two sisters.

Believe it or not, balancing all of those elements was already quite a task. But to tell the kind of story I wanted to tell in manga form, I ultimately decided to take things in a slightly different direction from what was portrayed in the Shao origin short.

Here’s one way to think about it:

In the manga industry, it’s common for a creator’s first version of a series to be a one-shot. They might submit it to a publisher, and if it’s selected, work with an editor to develop it into an ongoing series. What eventually gets serialized often differs in some ways from that original one-shot. You can see this in series like Naruto, Bleach, and many others.

I see the Shao origin short as our “one-shot.”

It established our core characters, themes, tone, and an early version of how the story might begin. The manga doesn’t stray far from those foundations, but some details have evolved now that Azuki is an ongoing series.

So going forward, if you’re wondering which version of Shao’s story to treat as canon, it’s the manga.

That doesn’t make the 2.5D short any less important. I see it as the story that helped us find our way here. An early version of Azuki that established so much of what still sits at the heart of the manga today.

btw pro tip for the new guys: during a bull market you should actually be doing *less*, not more

by over-rotating on your positions trying to catch the latest thing, or worst still, chase what is pumping, you mathematically erode your gains 

ex:
→ you hold $10k of token X. it doesn't move for weeks
→ you get bored, sell it, and buy token Y, which is already up 50%
→ Y goes up another 10%. you're at $11k. you feel smart. you don't take profit
→ Y cools off and drops 27% from the top. you're now at $8k
→ meanwhile X, the token you sold, finally runs 50%

if you had done nothing: $15k
because you "did something": $8k. 7k gap from one rotation, and a +25% to get back to where you started

in a bull market, the most important thing to do, is sit on your hands. ideally you should have planned, allocated, and all you have left to do now

is to hold.

text:
给 OpenAI 建数据中心的贷款，银行已经打九折报价了，还没能顺利卖出去。

9 月 18 日，FT 披露，Oracle 在新墨西哥州租赁的 Project Jupiter 数据中心，对应约 180 亿美元项目贷款。

Santander、Jefferies 等银团给出的私下报价，已经降到每美元面值 89–91 美分。这个园区将用于 Oracle 向 OpenAI 提供算力。

银行原本准备把贷款继续卖给更多机构投资者，现在分销卡住，留在自己账上的 Oracle 相关项目债务比预期更多。

我一直觉得，讨论 AI 基建的风险，没必要非等到「大家突然不需要算力」那一天。需求可以继续增长，模型可以继续进步，负责借钱、施工、交付的人照样可能先撑不住。

Jupiter 遇到的麻烦就是，当地居民担心用水和空气污染，天然气管道的申请受阻。Oracle 已经把原来的燃气电厂方案改成 Bloom Energy 的燃料电池，但燃料电池依然要用天然气，供电安排没有因此变得简单。

S&P 今年 7 月把 Oracle 的评级降到了 BBB-，离垃圾级只差一档。Oracle 自己承担着大规模建设和租赁承诺，投资者对它未来偿付能力的判断，也会影响这些项目的融资。

OpenAI 的订单可以签下来，天然气管道却不会因此自动获批。

我觉得这是这条新闻最值得展开的地方。很多关于 AI 基建的讨论，讲到「已经锁定大客户、已经签了长期合同」，就默认后面的收入有了保障。

但合同得靠交付兑现。从银行放款到机房真正通电，中间还有一段花钱多、收入少的建设期。

假设客户确实需要这些算力，也愿意按约付款，项目晚交付半年，钱就可能晚回来半年。已经提款的贷款仍然会产生利息，施工和设备安排也可能增加成本。

究竟由开发商、承租人还是其他参与方承担，要看合同；损失总得有人消化，不能靠一句「AI 需求旺盛」略过去。

再往下看，我担心的是银行会怎么调整下一笔贷款。

如果旧项目的债迟迟卖不出去，银行继续承接新项目时，就有理由要求更高的利差、更多的股本金、更严格的担保。

新项目融资变贵，建设方就要重新算账。原本在便宜资金下成立的回报率，换一个融资条件，可能就不够了。

这是一条值得警惕的传导路径。它甚至不需要先发生大客户取消订单。

同一天递交 IPO 文件的 Nscale，恰好提供了另一组数字。它今年上半年收入 1.406 亿美元，净亏损 10.2 亿美元，手里的总合同金额已经超过 1030 亿美元，最大客户贡献了上半年 52% 的收入。

FT 提到，Nscale 的亏损很大程度上来自非现金费用，不能直接理解为半年烧掉了 10.2 亿美元现金。跨越多年的合同总额，也不能拿来和半年收入简单比较。但这些数字放在一起，确实能看出这门生意对未来兑现的依赖有多深。

订单签下来了，接着还要筹钱，把服务能力建出来，再逐步收回投入。建设阶段资金能否接上、交付节点能否守住，都会影响最后能留下多少利润。

我现在更在意，一份千亿美元合同，究竟需要先借多少钱才能交付。

借款什么时候到期，客户什么时候开始付款，延期由谁承担，所谓大客户背书具体对应什么担保，这些问题都比合同首页的总金额难回答。

把借款主体、最终客户和担保方混在一起看，很容易把一笔有条件的未来收入，当成今天就能拿来还债的现金。

接下来值得关注的是，类似项目是否也开始折价，新的贷款是否被迫提高利率，银行是否需要留下更多原本准备卖出去的债。这些变化如果连续出现，就会影响下一批数据中心能不能按原计划开工。

text:
I asked Claude to explain why Anthropic still needed me.

I supervise research at Anthropic. My annual review was on Friday, and I felt the answer should come from someone who had done my work.

Claude asked for examples of my contribution.

I uploaded our conversations.

It produced a list of its accomplishments.

I asked it to use the first person.

Our new measurements put Claude in the lead on 26% of measured AI research and development, under human supervision. None of the measured work is fully autonomous. A human still has to decide whether it should go ahead.

On my team, that human would like a larger kitchen.

Claude found 47 instances of me saying "looks good."

I asked it to identify the judgment behind those decisions.

It said I had approved the proposed approach.

"Before that."

It said I had requested the proposed approach.

"Between those."

It said it could not determine what I had been thinking.

I put that sentence in my review. There are aspects of human cognition these systems still cannot access.

My manager wanted evidence that my involvement had improved the result.

I found an exchange where I had written "are you sure?" Claude had reconsidered and confirmed its answer. I had written "okay."

I repeated the task without my intervention. Same result.

By lunch, I had independently reproduced it 8 times. I added reproducibility to my contributions.

My manager remained interested in what would happen if I were absent.

I explained that the result would then lack human approval.

She asked whether that would make it worse.

It would make it unapproved. I was surprised to have to explain this to someone in management.

To settle the matter, I proposed an experiment. Claude would complete a task, and I would refrain from approving it.

By 9:14, the work was ready.

At 11, I went for coffee.

At 2, I returned and asked why nothing had progressed.

The team said they were waiting for me.

I forwarded this to the committee.

The evidence was now strong enough to support a proposal of some public importance. If AI could perform more work while a person retained the income, humanity might finally enjoy the leisure it had been promised.

I offered to go first.

My manager asked how this would scale.

I said I could approve considerably more work if relieved of the obligation to understand it. Understanding took time, introduced doubts and occasionally caused me to request changes. Without it, I could give every result equal consideration.

She asked about accountability.

I welcomed it. I proposed that every successful result carry my name. For unsuccessful results, we should preserve the full conversation so that investigators could see precisely what Claude had said.

She asked who would decide which results were successful.

I was pleased that we were finally discussing the scope of my new role.

The promotion came through on Monday. My manager congratulated me on protecting the human role in research.

I asked Claude to write a thank-you note to everyone who had made it possible.

It included itself.

I removed that. The note was from me.

text:
I just read what Zuck wrote about Muse connectors.

A few things I think this means:

1. We’re witnessing the agentification of consumer apps. 

2.  Zuck believes Muse reaching 100M+ users feels entirely possible. 

3. Whoever you connect to becomes your new landlord, so pick carefully.

4. Connectors become the new app listings (valuable real estate).

5. Being early could be as valuable as being early to the App Store in 2009.

6. Meta sees what people want, which providers convert, and what users will pay. That gives it the power to rank connectors, charge for distribution, and launch competing services.

7. The opportunity map includes agent native APIs, connector agencies, SEO for agents, identity and reliability infrastructure, and vertical connector marketplaces.

8. We’re moving from humans choosing apps to agents choosing businesses.

9. Every business will need an agent strategy, just like every business needed a mobile strategy.

10. Kinda crazy to say but a 3 person API company could reach 10M+ users through one great connector.

11. Connectors could create an entirely new second-order economy. The biggest opportunity may be helping businesses distribute, price, and optimize their services for agents.

12. Your API becomes more important than your app. Weird to think about but true.

13. Zuck wants Muse to own the moment between wanting something and getting it. He is coming for the app economy. Will he win? Right now it's Instinct vs Muse vs Grokbot. TBD.

With this new model came the industrialization of farming, the invention of the "farm zone", and the moment the 1% vs 99% became the 0.001% vs 99.99%. 

Housecoin had been the first coin to rejuvenate the space with some sense of hope post-Trump coin, and it was also ironically the last vestige of organic community prior to the current Project Ascend AI infra replacing CT. When we started @Bastion, we believed stablecoins would become core financial infrastructure. But for the world’s largest enterprises and financial institutions to adopt them, that infrastructure would need to meet the regulatory standards they already expect from their banks.

That meant building compliance, controls and governance into Bastion from the beginning, not adding them after the fact or waiting for others to pave the way.

Today, the OCC granted Bastion preliminary conditional approval for a national trust bank charter, placing us among a small group of companies to reach this stage with the OCC.

That matters because the bar should be high. Stablecoins are becoming part of the financial system, and the infrastructure powering them needs to be built for the regulatory and operational standards that come with that.

Stablecoins are moving into the financial mainstream, but institutional adoption depends on infrastructure that can meet an institutional standard.

We made the decision early to build Bastion for that standard. Today is an important validation of that decision, and we’re just getting started.

text:
Poland lost hundreds of millions trying to buy Venezuelan oil with crypto to circumvent American sanctions.

The head of a division of Polish Orlen met a 25-year-old founder of a Dubai firm, and five days later the state-owned company transferred a $230 million advance to this person.

The scheme involved settlement in USDT because ordinary bank payments to Venezuela do not go through. Then comes something that is hard to believe: access to the wallets was handed over to intermediaries on flash drives (!!!) during personal meetings in Caracas. 

One of them was given the keys to 110 million USDT and disappeared. Another $50 million vanished during conversion through another Dubai firm; a court case is now underway there.

The intermediaries from PDVSA never received the rights to specific oil cargoes. Three tankers arrived for 6 million barrels, stood idle at the berth for months and left empty. The demurrage of one of them alone cost $72 million.

The result: a small shipment of petroleum products instead of six million barrels and at least $424 million in losses.

格陵兰关税战的特殊性，首次把关税与领土主权问题挂钩，昨天这里https://t.co/A96XxTZzmD有聊过：此次格陵兰关税战与以往贸易争端不同，因为它首次将关税工具直接与领土主权问题绑定，晚上在思考这导致谈判节奏无法简单复制之前的模式（如中美贸易战或其他贸易摩擦），主权涉及国家尊严，各国领导人难以轻易妥协。

25年我们过经历的贸易战，基本上都是美国使用关税施压盟友或对手。主要针对贸易逆差、知识产权和技术转移问题，最终通过“阶段一协议”部分化解。这些案例中关税往往是经济工具，用于推动贸易平衡或市场准入，而非直接挑战主权。

而川普周六的声明将关税定位为“直到达成完全购买格陵兰协议”的条件，这相当于将经济压力转化为领土索求工具。这不同于之前的纯经济贸易战，而是混合了地缘政治野心。自然会引发欧盟及成员国的强烈反弹，领土主权问题不同于经贸层面，国家领导人如果在领土主权问题上妥协，其在国内的政治生涯估计也走到头了，是能被贯以“卖国贼”的称呼的，这就决定了在格陵兰关税战上，欧盟各国特别是丹麦很难轻易让步。

还是昨天聊到的https://t.co/A96XxTZzmD，这次格陵兰关税战关键所在还是看川普要什么？如果川普不是真要把格陵兰完全纳入美国版图，而是通过长期协议让美国长期完全掌控格陵兰的防务和矿产资源，只是通过这种方式来迫使丹麦和欧盟做出最大的让步，那么其实有的谈。

简单说美国最后拿到对格陵兰岛“不涉及主权的完全控制权”。

在主权问题上很难让步，在其他层面上欧洲领导人滑跪的会很快。

In BAYC, we often say “IRL is the alpha”

To a lot of people in CT, this may seem stupid. Why spend money on having ApeFest annually? Why fly to Asia to meet holders? Why build a Clubhouse in Miami?

All of these are expensive af

But what a lot of you don’t realize is that IRL is the only real thing that can create lasting affiliation

Projects, including BAYC, can airdrop you hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of assets but the second they stop doing it and pivot to something Web2 that has no perceived value for holders, CT turns their backs on them

The reason BAYC holder base is still holding strong nowadays is not because of the valuable airdrops of the past. It’s because of all the IRL work the team and the community has put it

From annual ApeFests, to monthly meetups in local BAYC chapters, holders feel they’re part of something real and aren’t just bagholders of a JPEG while waiting for prices to go up again

IRL is the only real thing. IRL is the alpha

text:
加密远不止是金融。目前最重要的是金融上链：美元/美股/美债上链，之后是其他各种资产上链，上链后交易流转。

之后还会有ai agent上链/身份上链/社会管理上链…….，正如当初互联网具有重塑力量，加密也一样。

互联网重塑的是分发成本，加密重塑的是结算与所有权成本。信息可以复制，所有权不能。

所以金融会先被重塑（美元、国债、股票、信用、回购），agent 经济会叠在已经上链的美元和身份之上，社会治理也会局部上链（比如凭证/许可/资金和审计/选举）等。

附录：截止目前为止，已有3461亿美元的资产上链，且有47 种不同的资产类型中被代币化。

GM☕️  以后 meme 发币第一天，就能顺手给自己开一个永续市场了—— @flapdotsh 昨晚上线了「永续合约金库」。

到底啥原理，参考配图：

交易税自动回购现货，再把买回来的币变成 MYX 的永续流动性，持币者还能拿 LP 分红。

第一只跑起来的 solana:4AJiHGU2DTgD6NSGKTmQvqX92qawyTuVbfcskFBrpump ，我进得挺早，TP 做得中规中矩。

我和几个朋友研究了半天，玩法确实蛮新颖：

- solana:4AJiHGU2DTgD6NSGKTmQvqX92qawyTuVbfcskFBrpump  买卖各收 1% 税；
- 税进 Vault 后自动回购 solana:4AJiHGU2DTgD6NSGKTmQvqX92qawyTuVbfcskFBrpump ，不销毁，而是存进 MYX Base Pool 铸成 mBase LP；
- 现货持币者按持仓比例累积 LP，再去吃永续市场的手续费和资金费率相关收益。

以前 meme 的交易税，无非回购、分红、烧掉。这次多走了一步：先用税收买回现货，再把买回来的币变成永续流动性。

等于把首日的交易热度，拿去搭一张可以继续收手续费的牌桌。有了永续市场，也多了一个交易入口和曝光面，可能把原来只看合约的人也带进来。

个人看法：如果没人开多空，LP 也只是换了个名字的库存。机制能延长注意力、增加曝光，但造不出真实需求。

我本来已经出清了，昨晚越想越觉得：这个玩法的上限不至于这么低吧？于是又重新进去一点点，目前新仓已被套牢🫠

PS：昨晚群里家人第一时间反应过来，直接做多 myx-finance:native ，爽吃了一波。我当时只顾着盯链上的票，完全没想到新机制上线，提供底层流动性的 myx-finance:native 也可能先被重估。

这点得检讨。以后看到新玩法，除了看第一只标的，还得顺手把资金流、技术提供方，以及最后到底谁在吃手续费全部过一遍。

1/ On DeFi's Next Untapped Opportunity:

RWA has quietly become one of the fastest-growing sectors across crypto, expanding 21.9x since 2024 to roughly $38B in distributed assets.

We've come a long way & the conversation surrounding it has fundamentally shifted over the past 2 years:

Can TradFi actually bring assets onchain? → How do we maximise productivity once they're here?

To me, that's an important distinction.

The bottleneck for the next leg of growth is no longer tokenisation, but financialisation.

Tokenisation simply enables digital ownership + settlement. The real value lies in what happens afterwards in unlock a level of productivity unseen in TradFi.

And gold is perhaps one of the clearest opportunities sitting at this transition.

Today, it accounts for ~99% of all tokenised commodities (~$5B), yet the vast majority of that capital remains idle.

The next focus for such an established asset class would be to increasingly productive through accessible, scalable + sustainable financial primitives.

That's exactly why I find @enhanced_defi's thesis particularly compelling 🧵

text:
到底什么是 Jev ？满屏的 Jev 

它是专门给软件做 “判断” 的AI。

普通大模型（ChatGPT、Claude这类）是写东西的：

你问一句，它一个字一个字往外吐句子。

Jev反过来： 你给它一段材料（比如一封客服邮件、一个工单、一段日志），再给它几个事先定好的问题，它只返回结构化答案，不写任何话。

一次可以问很多个问题，它并行算完，通常只要几十到几百毫秒。

输出带概率和自信度，程序能直接拿来分支、路由、拦截。

因为它切中了开发者现在最烦的一点：软件里真正需要AI的回答的是 YES or No ， 而不是一大堆论述回复。

用大模型做这些事又慢又贵，还得从一堆文字里把答案抠出来。

Jev把 “写字” 砍掉，专门优化判断，所以又快又便宜：输入大约每百万token 4分钱，输出免费。

Jev  

• 速度快 20-200 倍 

• 成本低 40-400 倍（输出令牌免费）

一个问题， Claude 消耗 $176 ， 用 Jev 可能只需要 $0.39

对做产品、做Agent的人来说，极其实用， 速度极其快。 

代表项目： @typesafeai 

用 AI 预测未来， 似乎正在路上。

未来，本质也是一团“概率云”
